opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that humans don't come to these tasks as blank slates. When you pick up a new video game, you already know what a wall is, that falling is bad, that a key probably opens a door, that the thing moving toward you might be an enemy. You bring years of priors about physics, objects, cause and effect, even the conventions of game design. So "easy for humans" really means easy given an enormous amount of pre-training that we just don't notice.

A standard RL agent starts with almost nothing. It sees pixels or a state vector, takes random actions, and gets a scalar reward, often very sparse. In something like Montezuma's Revenge, you might need a long, precise sequence of actions before you see any reward at all. Random exploration basically never stumbles onto it, so the agent has no signal to learn from. That's the exploration problem, and it's still one of the hardest parts of RL.

Then there's credit assignment. Even when a reward does arrive, the agent has to figure out which of the hundreds of earlier actions actually mattered. Humans do this with causal reasoning: "I got the points because I jumped over that thing." The agent has to infer it statistically from lots and lots of trials.

Sample efficiency follows from all of this. A person might get decent at an Atari game in fifteen minutes. Early deep RL agents needed tens of millions of frames, the equivalent of days or weeks of nonstop play. Control tasks are similar: a kid learns to balance or grab things through a rich body and lots of sensory feedback, whereas a simulated robot is optimizing a reward function that may not even capture what we really want, and it'll happily exploit any loophole in it.

There's also an engineering side people underestimate. RL is notoriously sensitive to hyperparameters, random seeds, and small implementation details. Two "identical" algorithms can behave very differently because of how advantages are normalized or how the environment is wrapped. That's part of why I cared so much about building clean, fast, reproducible infrastructure: a lot of what looks like "the algorithm doesn't work" is actually "the pipeline is fragile."

So the gap isn't that games are secretly hard. It's that RL tries to learn everything from reward alone, while humans lean on prior knowledge, good exploration instincts, and reasoning. That's also why things got so much more interesting once we started combining RL with large pre-trained models. Suddenly the agent starts with some of those priors, and RL becomes more about refining behavior than discovering everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response explains that tasks are easy for humans because they bring years of prior knowledge about physics, objects, cause and effect, and game conventions, while standard RL agents start with almost nothing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "easy for humans" is a bit of an illusion. When a person sits down at a new game, they're not starting from zero. They already know that objects fall, that a door is for walking through, that a ladder means climbing, that a thing chasing you is probably bad. They've spent years building a model of how the world works, and a game just borrows from that. An RL agent gets none of it. It sees a grid of pixels, or a vector of joint angles, and it has to discover all of that structure from scratch, purely from reward.

And reward is a terribly thin signal. In Montezuma's Revenge, for example, you might take thousands of actions before you see a single point. From the agent's perspective, almost everything it does gets the same feedback: nothing. So the exploration problem is really the core of it. Humans explore with intent, we have hypotheses, we try the obvious thing first. The agent is mostly adding noise to its actions and hoping something interesting happens.

Then there's the data question. A human can learn a game in maybe twenty minutes of play. The classic Atari agents needed tens of millions of frames, which is weeks of continuous play. That's part of why I spent so much effort on infrastructure, on things like EnvPool, because if you can't run environments fast enough, you simply can't do the research. Sample efficiency is still an open problem, and we partly compensate with raw throughput.

The control side has its own version of this. The physical world is continuous, long-horizon, and partially observable. A robot arm has to coordinate many joints at once, and a tiny error early in a trajectory compounds. Humans get motor skills for free through evolution and childhood. We're asking an algorithm to reproduce that with a loss function.

And finally, the reward itself is fragile. Agents are extremely good at finding the easiest way to maximize the number you gave them, which is often not the behavior you wanted. So part of the difficulty isn't the algorithm, it's that we as designers are bad at specifying what "good" means. Humans fill in that gap with common sense. The agent only has what's in the equation.

So I don't think of it as RL being weak. I think of it as RL being asked to solve a much harder problem than the one the human is actually solving.

r001.rationale: The response says humans bring years of learned knowledge about how the world works, while an RL agent must discover that structure from scratch.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of what looks easy for humans is easy because we bring so much prior experience. When we play a new game, we already have intuitions about objects, movement, and cause and effect. We can read the instructions and form a reasonable strategy before taking any action.

A reinforcement learning agent often has to learn those things through trial and error, with a reward signal that can be very sparse. If it succeeds or fails after hundreds of actions, which actions were responsible? And if it never discovers a successful strategy, it may get very little feedback about how to improve.

Control adds another challenge: actions change what the agent will encounter next. A small mistake can put it in a situation it has never seen before, and then it has to recover. Humans also make mistakes, but we can draw on experience from other situations. So the difficulty is partly learning a task, but also learning useful representations, exploring effectively, and transferring knowledge—all things we tend to take for granted when we call a task easy.

r001.rationale: The response says humans bring substantial prior experience and intuitions about objects, movement, and cause and effect, while reinforcement learning agents must learn these through trial and error.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that what feels easy to us often relies on a lot of experience we take for granted. When we play a new game, we already have intuitions about objects, movement, and cause and effect. We can use those intuitions to decide what to try. A reinforcement learning agent may have to learn all of that through interaction, with only a reward signal telling it whether it did well.

There’s also the problem of delayed feedback. You might make a decision now and only discover much later whether it helped. The agent has to figure out which actions deserve credit, while also deciding whether to explore something new or repeat something that already works. So a task can look very simple from the outside, but learning it from scratch can require a huge amount of trial and error.

r001.rationale: The response says apparently easy tasks rely on experience and intuitions humans take for granted, which an RL agent may need to learn through interaction.
